video_title: The $2B AI Startup Simulating Human Behavior with 85% Accuracy
gist: Simile CEO (Stanford researcher behind the Smallville generative-agents work) explains how the $2B company builds a foundation model of human behavior, trained on large real-human panels, that simulates surveys and consumer decisions at a claimed 85%+ accuracy for enterprises like CVS. Largely a founder pitch: strong on mechanism and data-moat framing, light on revenue disclosure.

insights.claim: Simile is building a foundation model of human behavior that takes a description of a person or group and simulates what they would do in a given context, sold as a SaaS web interface where users define who to talk to and what to ask, with no cap on questions.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Positions Simile as a horizontal behavior-simulation layer, not a chatbot or reasoning-model competitor.

insights.claim: Initial wedge is replacing traditional market research (surveys, concept testing, conjoint and max-diff analysis) that cost hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars over years, now run near-instantly as a query.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Targets the insights and market-research budget; incumbents in panels and survey tooling face cost-compression risk.
insights.quote: They are just a query away.

insights.claim: Simile keeps vertical-specific pre-built 'agent banks' (simulated panels) available on day one, then collects extra data to train on a customer's own unique population.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Reusable panels plus custom fine-tuning is a data-network-effect structure that lowers onboarding friction and raises switching costs.

insights.claim: Customers named include CVS (store layout, messaging, decor), large financial institutions, Banco in Brazil (policy and values messaging), entertainment and CPG companies; retail is currently the largest vertical.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Early traction is in large consumer-facing enterprises with heavy research budgets.

insights.claim: Beyond surveys, the roadmap is to simulate the environment as well as people, including competing options and alternatives, so that behavior such as price sensitivity can be predicted given the full context.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Moves from replacing research to scenario and pricing simulation, a much larger decision-support TAM.

insights.claim: Simile also targets internal stakeholders: simulating employee retention among top performers and how to recruit Stanford and MIT talent, done with informed consent.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: HR and talent is a secondary expansion area with privacy sensitivity.

insights.claim: In an experiment concluded at end of 2024, agents trained on voice interviews of 1,000 US-representative people predicted those same people's survey and behavioral-study responses two weeks later with 85%+ accuracy.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: This is the empirical foundation for the company; note the benchmark is predicting survey and study responses, not field behavior at scale.
insights.quote: we could actually show that we can predict people's behavior with 85% plus accuracy

insights.claim: Simile jointly trains a predictive model of accuracy that outputs a 0-100 confidence per response, analogous to a p-value; customers found confidence above roughly 85-90% robust enough for high-stakes decisions.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Calibrated confidence scores are what make simulation output decision-grade and auditable for enterprise buyers.

insights.claim: Evaluation evolved from 'believability' (human judges comparing agent answers to human-written ones in the 25-agent Smallville game town) to 'faithfulness and accuracy' against real people's later responses.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Shows an academic-to-commercial validation path; faithfulness to ground truth is the metric that matters for buyers.

insights.claim: Simulation must be grounded in large real-human data operations and evaluated alongside real people; it is not created 'out of vacuum'.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: The moat is the proprietary data operation (interviews, RCTs, panels), not just model architecture.

insights.claim: Simile has partnerships with over 40 million real people across global panels, talks to tens to hundreds of thousands of real people every week, and can source new panel members within 24 hours; Gallup (panel of hundreds of thousands) is a strategic partner.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Panel partnerships plus continuous fresh collection are the data moat and a ground-truth refresh loop.

insights.claim: Training data is built from voice-to-voice AI interviews (life stories, hard decisions) plus behavioral data; the most valuable data is randomized control trials varying one feature or message, because they reveal causal mechanism rather than correlation.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Causal experiment data is scarce and defensible; observational data like transactions and mobility is less valuable.
insights.quote: But what really matters is actually the causer mechanism

insights.claim: Survey quality controls include spacing out participation to avoid respondent fatigue and gaming, attention checks such as simple arithmetic or recall questions, and requiring informed consent, so minors are excluded as a known blind spot.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Known limits: underage populations are not covered, and panel bias is managed rather than eliminated.

insights.claim: Stated survey intentions roughly follow a normal distribution while actual action has an exponential-like activation-energy curve (e.g., saying 5-6 out of 7 on going to the gym vs. actually going), and the modeling challenge is learning this translation layer.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Explains why naive survey-based forecasts overstate behavior; a model of the say-do gap is the core IP.
insights.quote: The activation energy for me to actually go to the gym is actually way higher than what I would expect

insights.claim: Optionality and opportunity cost, not abstract preference, govern real behavior: the same offer is accepted in a vacuum but rejected when alternatives exist, which is why a sole water seller could charge a fortune but widely available water cannot.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Supports pricing and competitive-response simulation; surveys without competitive context mislead.

insights.claim: Some traits such as risk tolerance are not known to change in a person, so once learned they become highly predictable inputs to simulation.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Stable traits give a persistent basis for digital twins, while irrational behavior is injected through economic games and RCT data.

insights.claim: Customers care less about predicting the future than about what to do to change it, so the product emphasis is causal mechanism and levers rather than forecasting.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Reframes the product from prediction to intervention design; cuts against the 'forecasting engine' framing.
insights.quote: people are actually not that interested in predicting the future

themes.theme: Counterintuitive simulation value and use cases

insights.claim: In a pre-Simile study with automotive companies, the winning EV launch messaging was found to shift perception of non-electric vehicles and lower sales across the whole market, an example of second-order effects only visible via simulation.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Pitches simulation as surfacing system-level, counterintuitive downstream effects that single-question surveys miss.

insights.claim: Aspirational targets include simulating climate-policy coordination among competing actors and UBI outcomes in an AGI-imminent scenario instead of running multi-year studies, inspired by Thomas Schelling's segregation model.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Policy simulation is a long-dated, non-commercial option value story rather than near-term revenue.

insights.claim: Simile's own simulator predicted that the host might ask whether we live in a simulation, and the CEO says he simulates conversations before meetings, offered as a product demo.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Anecdotal demonstration of audience and interviewer simulation; also used by the host to test titles and topics for the episode.

insights.claim: Simile argues it differs from frontier LLM labs, which optimize for reasoning, coding and math assistants, because it models the diversity of viewpoints, values, tastes and both good and bad human behaviors.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Carves a non-overlapping niche from OpenAI-style general models, though frontier labs could enter via persona simulation.

insights.claim: The CEO says simulation is in its 'GPT-4/4.5 era' and expects the space to reach where coding agents are today in about 1.5 to 2 years; he expects forward-deployed engineering to be the main battleground, citing stickier relationships among forward-deployed coding-agent companies.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Signals heavy services-plus-software go-to-market and a view that deployment depth, not model alone, drives defensibility.
insights.quote: simulation is basically in its GP GP4 GP4.5 era

insights.claim: Simile has about 100 employees, with roughly 20-25% in science (many Stanford labmates returning from frontier labs plus social-science methodologists), and recently hired a head of engineering from DoorDash.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Research-heavy team drawn from Percy Liang's Stanford group; talent pull from frontier labs is a positive signal.

insights.claim: Simile has raised about $300M total at a reported $2B valuation, backed by Index and Greenoaks plus angels Fei-Fei Li and Andrej Karpathy, with ties via Stanford co-founders Michael Bernstein and Percy Liang.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Elite academic network and angel base supports the credibility of the pitch; valuation is aggressive relative to disclosed traction.

insights.claim: Asked about a hypothetical $15B acquisition offer, the CEO did not rule it out but said Simile would continue only if there is an ambitious idea that only Simile can pursue, framing a long-term independent stance.
insights.speaker: Simile CEO
insights.so_what: Non-committal on exit; no signal of near-term sale intent.
insights.quote: offers you $15 billion to sell your company
